extracted.intended_audience: readers of the Public Advertiser; politically engaged English public (late 18th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Opinion/political letters (Junius) addressing public liberty, judicature, civic virtue, and practical politics; normative prescriptions for behaviour of patriots, magistrates, and institutions in 18th-century Britain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid internal divisions; preserve union
rubrics_metrics.description: No man laments more sincerely ... the unhappy differences which have arisen among the friends of the people, and divided them from each other. These differences are only advantageous to the common enemy of the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise reconciliation where possible; if reconciliation is impracticable, guard against worst effects of division by persuading partisans to be separately useful to the common cause. Avoid letting personal animosities weaken the movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain honour and honesty despite disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Honour and honesty must not be renounced, although a thousand modes of right and wrong were to occupy the degrees of morality between Zeno and Epicurus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not sacrifice fundamental personal virtues in political contests; reject tactics that degrade personal reputation even when political disagreement is acute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve fundamental religious principles amid sectarianism
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental principles of Christianity may still be preserved, though every zealous sectary adheres to his own exclusive doctrine, and pious ecclesiastics make it a part of their religion to persecute one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolerate doctrinal differences among co‑religionists; do not allow sectarian disputes to subvert shared fundamental values that support civic unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ men according to their abilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Let us employ these men in whatever departments their various abilities are best suited to, and as much to the advantage of the common cause, as their different inclinations will permit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign political actors to roles matching talents and inclinations; accept separate usefulness rather than demanding total conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value leaders who depend on public favour
rubrics_metrics.description: That he has no possible resource but in the public favour, is, in my judgment, a considerable recommendation of him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer popular leaders who rely on the people's support (because dependence on public favour reduces likelihood of private betrayals or court corruption).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate republican manners among the people
rubrics_metrics.description: I would have the manners of the people purely and strictly republican ... a general attachment to the commonweal, distinct from any partial attachment to persons or families; an implicit submission to the laws only; and an affection to the magistrate, proportioned to the integrity and wisdom with which he distributes justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage civic virtues: loyalty to public good over personalities, obedience to law rather than to individuals, and respect for magistrates tied to demonstrated justice and competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reject assistance because of a single differing opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: That we should not generally reject the friendship or services of any man, because he differs from us in a particular opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate contributions by their practical benefit to the community; accept useful measures or services regardless of origin or some doctrinal disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use unsteady allies strategically to prevent desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Let us profit by the assistance of such men while they are with us, and place them, if it be possible, in the post of danger, to prevent desertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When cooperating with unreliable or opportunistic allies, deploy them where their involvement reduces risk of defection and maximises short‑term benefit to the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribute offices according to individuals' virtues and abilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Let us distribute the virtues and abilities of individuals according to the offices they affect; and, when they quit the service, let us endeavour to supply their places with better men than we have lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match personnel to roles and plan for replacement — do not expect perfection but manage succession and improvement of officeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refuse trivial compensation for essential injuries
rubrics_metrics.description: Let me guard my countrymen against the meanness and folly of accepting of a trifling or moderate compensation for extraordinary and essential injuries ... they magnify their generosity, when they give us baubles of little proportionate value for ivory and gold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept minimal concessions or symbolic gestures in return for substantial losses or rights; be wary of small compensations designed to placate while preserving an underlying injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on king's right to compel service (pressing seamen)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only case in which the king can have a right to arm his subjects in general, is that of a foreign force being actually landed upon our coast. ... With regard to the press for seamen, they may be softened by bounties, but when reasonable expense is incurred and bounties exhausted, the spur of the press is wanted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat compulsory military service as a last resort, justified only by imminent invasion; first exhaust voluntary measures (increased bounties) and regard pressing as a necessary expedient when those fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question legality of executive proclamations lacking parliamentary sanction
rubrics_metrics.description: If, in the interval between publishing such a proclamation ... and its receiving the sanction of the two houses, of what nature is it? Is it legal or illegal? ... If it be illegal, the subject is not bound to obey it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat orders/proclamations issued by the executive before parliamentary sanction as legally suspect; where possible challenge their legality through litigation or refuse obedience if clearly unlawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance public safety with defence of individual legal liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: I lament the unhappy necessity, whenever it arises, of providing for the safety of the state by a temporary invasion of the personal liberty of the subject. I regard the legal liberty of the meanest man in Britain as much as my own, and would defend it with the same zeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defend individual legal rights vigorously, but recognise that in exceptional circumstances limited, temporary infringements of liberty may be necessary for the safety of the state; always seek reconciliation of these objectives where practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve liberty of the press; abuses must be checked by jury not forfeiture
rubrics_metrics.description: The liberty of the press may be abused, and the abuse of a valuable privilege is the certain means to lose it'—I deny that. Let the abuse be submitted to a jury; a sufficient, and, indeed, the only legal and constitutional check upon the license of the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect freedom of the press against broad suppressive measures. Address abuses through legal process (jury trials) rather than by stripping the public of the privilege.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion civil damages to rank and fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: That the damages should be proportioned to the rank and fortune of the parties ... because what is a compensation or penalty to one man, is none to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set monetary remedies so they are effective relative to the defendant's means/position; equal nominal damages may be meaningless if not proportional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal jurisprudence should rely on positive law and precedent, not scripture or foreign codes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bible is the code of our religious faith, not of our municipal jurisprudence: ... an English jury have nothing to do either with David or the prophet. They consider the crime only as it is a breach of order, an injury to an individual, and an offence to society; and they judge of it by certain positive rules of law, or by the practice of their ancestors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground legal decisions in established common law, statutes, and precedent rather than religious texts or imported legal systems when judging domestic civil/criminal matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Before condemning contested practices, examine judicial and parliamentary record
rubrics_metrics.description: General warrants ... had never been regularly questioned or resisted, until the case of Mr. Wilkes. ... Press warrants ... have been complained of, questioned, and resisted in a thousand instances; but still the legislature have never interposed, nor has there ever been a formal decision against them in any of the superior courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticising or seeking reform of practices (e.g., press warrants), first review existing judicial opinions, statutes, and parliamentary actions; base arguments on strong facts and authoritative reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magistrate's dual duty: guard liberty and provide for community safety
rubrics_metrics.description: The magistrate who guards the liberty of the individual deserves to be commended. But let him remember, that it is also his duty to provide for, or at least not to hazard, the safety of the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public officials must weigh individual freedoms against collective security; in scenarios like imminent invasion, prefer measures that secure the community even if they constrain individual liberty.
